title: Everyday Object Functions
theme: Answering what a familiar object is used for
materials: Three or four very familiar real objects, such as a cup, a spoon, a toothbrush, a coat, or a favorite book.
instructions: Gather three or four objects your child uses every day. Hold up one object or point to it and ask a simple use question, such as "What do we use a cup for?" Pause for a few seconds and give your child time to answer. Accept any spoken answer that gives the use — "drinking", "for drinking", or "you drink" are all fine, and a short phrase is enough. Warmly say the whole answer back once, such as "Yes, we drink from a cup," then move to the next object. Keep it conversational and stop while your child is still enjoying it.
success_criteria: The child says what at least one object is used for. A single word or a short phrase counts when it accurately gives the use; the grammar does not need to be correct.
make_easier: Use only one or two of the most familiar objects. You may model the answer once — "We use a cup for drinking" — then ask again a moment later and give your child a chance to say it. A starter such as "We use it for..." can help. If your child only points to the object, shows you how it is used, or picks it up, acknowledge that warmly and say the words again, but wait for a spoken answer before counting it as success.
make_harder: Drop the starter and ask the open question. Use a familiar object whose use is a little less obvious, such as a towel or a lid. You can also ask about an object that is not in front of you.
group_play_line: A sibling can answer about one object, then pass the next object to your child to answer.
what_to_avoid: Do not ask the same question over and over until the answer is right — say the use yourself and move on. Never hold back something your child needs, such as a drink, a coat or a comfort item, while waiting for an answer.

title: Choose, Then Tell Me
theme: Choosing an object by its use, then saying what it is for
materials: Two familiar objects with clearly different uses, such as a cup and a shoe, or a spoon and a toothbrush.
instructions: Put two familiar objects where your child can see both. Ask which one is used for a purpose, such as "Which one do we use for drinking?" and let your child choose. Then ask the question that matters: "What do we use it for?" Pause and give your child time to answer in words. Accept any spoken answer that gives the use, say it back warmly once, and then try a different pair. Play a few rounds while your child is interested.
success_criteria: After choosing, the child says what the object is used for. The choice itself is scaffolding and does not count on its own — the spoken answer is the success.
make_easier: Use two objects whose uses are very different. You may model the answer once and then ask again. You can also offer two spoken answers to pick between, such as "Is it for drinking or for sleeping?", so your child still answers in words.
make_harder: Drop the choice and simply hand your child one object, asking what it is for. You can also use two objects whose uses sit closer together, such as a spoon and a fork.
group_play_line: One child picks the object and the other says what it is for, then they switch.
what_to_avoid: Do not treat a correct choice as the answer and move on — that skips the part you are practising. Do not keep asking if your child does not answer; say the use yourself and carry on.

title: What Do We Need?
theme: Answering a use question inside an everyday routine
materials: No special materials — use something you already do each day, such as brushing teeth, getting dressed, washing hands, or getting ready to go outside.
instructions: At the start of a familiar part of the day, say what you are about to do and ask what is needed. For example, "We are going to brush our teeth. What do we need?" or "We are going outside and it is cold. What do we need?" Pause and give your child time to answer. Accept any spoken answer that names a useful item or gives its use, such as "toothbrush", "my coat", or "keeps me warm." Say the answer back warmly once and carry on. Ask one question per occasion so it stays part of the day rather than a quiz.
success_criteria: The child says what is needed, or what it is for, at least once. A single accurate word counts.
make_easier: Ask while the item is already in sight. You may model the answer once and ask again the next time it comes round. A starter such as "We need our..." can help. If your child fetches the item without speaking, that shows they understand — acknowledge it, name the item and its use, and wait for a spoken answer before counting success.
make_harder: Ask before the items are in sight, so your child answers from the situation rather than from what they can see. You can also add a short follow-up about the use: "And what is it for?"
group_play_line: A sibling can answer first at the same moment of the day, then your child takes the next turn.
what_to_avoid: Never delay or hold back something your child needs — a coat, a toothbrush, food, the bathroom — while waiting for an answer. Hand it over, name it, and ask again another day. Do not stretch out what you are doing to fit more questions in.

title: Silly Function Mix-Up
theme: Correcting a playful mix-up and saying the real use
materials: Two or three very familiar objects, such as a spoon, a shoe, a hat, or a cup.
instructions: Pick up a familiar object and say something deliberately silly about what it is for, such as "Do we wear a spoon on our feet?" Look playful and pause — most children will protest or laugh. Then ask the real question: "So what do we use a spoon for?" Give your child time to answer in words. Accept any spoken answer that gives the real use, say it back warmly once, and move on to another mix-up. Keep every mix-up obvious and gentle, and stop while it is still fun.
success_criteria: The child says what the object is really used for. Laughing or saying "no" is a good start but is not the success on its own; the spoken use is.
make_easier: Use the most familiar objects and the most obvious mix-ups. After your child protests, model the real answer once — "A spoon is for eating" — then ask again and give them a turn to say it.
make_harder: Make the mix-up a little less obvious, such as suggesting a towel is for drinking. You can also let your child invent a silly mix-up for you to correct, then ask them for the real use.
group_play_line: Take turns making the silly statement while the other person corrects it and says the real use.
what_to_avoid: Keep every mix-up harmless and clearly silly — never suggest something that could hurt your child if they tried it. The only thing being corrected is your own playful mistake, never your child. Stop if your child seems confused rather than amused.

title: Function From a Picture
theme: Answering what a pictured object is used for
materials: Clear photos or book pictures of familiar single objects — a cup, a bed, a coat, a toothbrush, a crayon.
instructions: Look at one picture together. Point to the object and ask what it is used for, such as "What do we use this for?" Pause and give your child time to answer in words. Accept any spoken answer that gives the use, say it back warmly once, and turn to another picture if your child is still interested. Keep the focus on what the object does rather than on its name — if your child names it instead, say the name back and then ask the use question again.
success_criteria: The child says what at least one pictured object is used for. Naming the object is not the success on its own; the use is.
make_easier: Start with the real object in your hands, ask the use question, then show a picture of the same object and ask again. One or two pictures is plenty. You may model the answer once before asking.
make_harder: Use pictures of objects your child has not practised, or a picture where the object sits in a busier scene. You can also ask without pointing, letting your child find the object first and then say its use.
group_play_line: A sibling can choose the next picture and say what the object is for, then give your child a turn.
what_to_avoid: Do not work through a stack of pictures like flash cards. A few meaningful pictures and a relaxed back-and-forth are better than a long session.

title: Tell Me Another One
theme: Giving a second everyday use for a familiar object
materials: One or two familiar objects with more than one clear everyday use, such as a towel, a chair, or paper.
instructions: Choose one familiar object with more than one obvious use. Ask what it is used for, such as "What do we use a towel for?" Pause and give your child time to answer. Accept any spoken answer that gives a real use and say it back warmly once. If your child is enjoying it, ask whether there is anything else we use it for, and accept a second use if it comes. One good answer is enough — a second use is a bonus, not the target.
success_criteria: The child says at least one real use for the object. A second use is welcome but is not required for success.
make_easier: Use an object with one very strong use and accept that answer without asking for another. You may model the first use once and then ask again.
make_harder: Ask for a second use after the first, or choose an object whose second use is less obvious, such as paper for drawing and for wrapping something. Keep both uses ones your child has really seen.
group_play_line: Take turns adding a use for the same object until you run out, keeping it playful rather than competitive.
what_to_avoid: Do not press for a second use once your child has given one. Do not accept a made-up or impossible use as correct — say the real one warmly instead and move on.

title: Mini Problem Solver
theme: Naming a useful object from a simple everyday situation
materials: No materials needed, though the objects you talk about should be ones your child already knows.
instructions: Describe a simple, familiar situation and ask what would help. For example, "My hands are wet. What could I use?" or "It is dark in here. What could I use?" or "I want to draw a picture. What do I need?" Pause and give your child time to answer in words. Accept any spoken answer that names a useful object or gives its use, such as "a towel" or "for drying." Say the answer back warmly once, then try another situation if your child is still interested. Keep every situation concrete and about things your child has really seen.
success_criteria: The child says a useful object, or what it is for, for at least one situation. A single accurate word counts.
make_easier: Use situations your child meets every day, and have the useful object visible in the room. You can offer two spoken options — "Could I use a towel or a cup?" — and let your child answer in words. You may also model one whole example first.
make_harder: Use a situation where the useful object is not in the room. You can also add a short follow-up about the use: "And what does a towel do?" Keep to everyday situations.
group_play_line: A sibling can answer one situation and then make up a simple situation for your child to answer.
what_to_avoid: Keep every situation ordinary and safe — never describe something frightening or risky to make the question interesting. Do not turn this into riddles, guessing games, or situations needing several steps of reasoning. If your child does not answer, say what you would use and move on.
